Styles / 14

Flat design

An interface style of about 2010–2016 that removed gradients, gloss, textures, and shadows from screens. Surfaces are solid fields of saturated color, type is a plain sans-serif that is often light, and icons are simple glyphs. This record covers the core of the style: Microsoft’s Metro design language and the flat web and app design that followed it. Material Design and “flat 2.0” are related branches that bring back some depth.

Clean / Bright / Direct / Digital

Visual grammar

  • No simulated depth. No gradients, gloss, bevels, textures, or drop shadows. A button is a solid color rectangle, and a panel is a solid color field.
  • Saturated solid fields. Several bright, clean hues, such as turquoise, blue, purple, orange, and red, fill whole bands, tiles, and buttons. Text is often a dark blue-gray instead of black, and the pale neutral is a cool gray.
  • Fills, not outlines. Areas separate by a change of fill color and by space. Borders are rare or absent.
  • Plain, often light sans-serif. Segoe UI in Metro, Helvetica Neue in iOS 7, and Lato or Open Sans on the web. Large headings are often light or regular weight. Zune and Windows Phone set titles in large lowercase letters.
  • Tiles and bands. Content sits in a grid of square or rectangular tiles, or in full-width color bands that stack down the page. Content replaces chrome.
  • Glyph icons and flat illustration. Single-color pictograms on colored squares or circles, and illustrations built from solid shapes. A 2013 branch adds long diagonal shadows to icons.
  • Motion instead of depth. Metro uses motion to show state and structure: live tiles change, pages slide, and presses and swipes get an animated response. Hover and press states on the web change the fill color.

What connects the references

Microsoft set the look. Windows Phone 7 introduced Metro in 2010; the Windows 8.1 Start screen and the Calculator app show its tiles, thin type, and single-accent controls, and Pentagram’s 2012 Windows logo applies the “authentically digital” rule to the brand mark. NN/g (2015) names Metro and Windows 8 as the main origin of the web trend.

The style reached Apple through third-party apps: Letterpress borrowed from Windows Phone, and Apple’s designers cited it for iOS 7. Apple’s own iOS 7 page shows thin type and flatter icons under a still-glossy navigation bar.

The web branch spread through free resources: Designmodo’s Flat UI kit with its named twenty-color palette, republished on Flat UI Colors; the free Lato typeface; flat icon sets such as Elegant Themes’ icons; and Metro UI CSS, which rebuilt Metro for the web.

Microsoft’s own sites of 2012–2013 are the clearest websites: Windows Azure, Windows Phone, Office.com, the Windows Dev Center, and windows.microsoft.com. Few non-Microsoft sites of the period kept a usable Wayback copy in the style; most tried copies lost their CSS or relied on photographs.

Captures calibrated the fingerprint. Many 2012–2014 pages draw tiles and bands with images, so computed-style color missed them; the fingerprint reads color from the screenshot instead (pixels.chromaticShare, pixels.hues). Hairline dividers and input borders are common, so the border limit is loose on share and strict on width. Light headings hold for Metro pages, but the Flat UI kit and windows.microsoft.com use bold headings (700 and 600), so the weight range describes the Metro branch more than the web branch.

Two branches bend the rules. The Elegant Themes icons add short solid shadows, a mild form of the 2013 long-shadow trend, and the Windows 8.1 tiles carry a faint gradient. Measurement cannot see gradients or shadows drawn in images, and archived pages often render in a fallback face because Segoe UI is not served, so judge archived pages with the rubric as well as the fingerprint.

Flat UI, Flat interface design, Metro (Microsoft design language)
Era
2010–2016. Microsoft introduced Metro with Windows Phone 7 in 2010. Zune (2006) and Windows Media Center (2002) show earlier elements. NN/g dates the web trend from about 2012. Material Design (2014) and Fluent (2017) add depth again, but flat interfaces stay common.

Name used by

Lineage

  • Influenced by International Typographic Style. Wikipedia names the International Typographic Style as the most substantial influence on flat design, and states that Metro is based on the principles of classic Swiss graphic design.
  • Influenced by Bauhaus. Wikipedia lists the styles that came from the Bauhaus among the influences on flat design.
  • Reaction against Skeuomorphism. NN/g (2015) describes flat design as a reaction against three-dimensional, skeuomorphic, and realistic styles. Microsoft’s documentation called Metro “authentically digital”. Apple’s iOS 7 (2013) replaced the textured interfaces of earlier versions.
  • Related to Metro (Microsoft design language). The core branch of this record. Wikipedia describes Metro as based on flat design: typography, simplified icons, no clutter, and basic geometric shapes, with transit signage as the stated inspiration. Its colored live tiles on Windows Phone 7 (2010) and Windows 8 (2012) are the clearest examples of the style.
  • Related to Material Design. Google’s design language of 2014. NN/g (2015) calls it “flat 2.0”: flat color and type, with shadows and card layers that show hierarchy. This record treats it as a related branch, not the core.
  • Related to Minimalist Machine. Both remove decoration. Minimalist Machine separates parts with thin outlines and monospaced labels. Flat design separates them with solid color fills.
  • Related to Neo-brutalism. Neo-brutalism keeps flat color but adds thick outlines and hard shadows. Its record treats it as a reaction against flat design.

Classification rubric

The test for a new reference

Identifies the style

  • Buttons, panels, and tiles are solid color fields with no gradient, gloss, or shadow.
  • Three or more saturated hues appear as fills, not only as text or icons.
  • Areas separate by fill color and space, not by outlines.
  • Type is a plain sans-serif, and large headings are light or regular weight.
  • Icons are single-color glyphs without shading.

Rules it out

  • Textures, gloss, bevels, or realistic materials.
  • Drop shadows or layered cards carry the hierarchy. This points to Material Design.
  • Thick black outlines or hard offset shadows.
  • Translucent, blurred panels.
  • A black-and-white page with one accent, where type and the grid carry the design.

Often confused with

International Typographic Style
The Swiss style is mostly black and white with one accent and relies on a grid and large bold type. Flat design fills large areas with several bright colors and often uses light headings.
Minimalist Machine
Minimalist Machine outlines its boxes with thin rules and uses monospaced labels on a neutral ground. Flat design separates areas by color fill and has almost no borders.
Bauhaus
Bauhaus uses the primary triad, heavy black bars, and circles, squares, and triangles as composition. Flat design uses a wider palette of clean secondary hues in plain rectangles and has no black bars.
Neo-brutalism
Neo-brutalism outlines every block in thick black and adds hard offset shadows. Flat design has neither.
Skeuomorphism
Skeuomorphism imitates materials with texture, gloss, and shadow. Flat design removes all of them.
Material Design
Material Design keeps flat color and type but lifts cards and buttons with soft shadows and uses a floating action button. Core flat design has no shadows.
Corporate Memphis
Corporate Memphis is a flat illustration style of people with large limbs. It can appear on a flat interface, but it is an illustration style, not an interface style.

Ideas to carry forward

  • Fill buttons, tiles, and bands with solid colors. Change the fill on hover and press.
  • Use three to five saturated hues with a dark blue-gray for text and a cool pale gray for quiet areas.
  • Separate areas with color and space. Leave out borders on cards and panels.
  • Use one plain sans-serif. Set large headings in a light or regular weight and keep labels semibold.
  • Arrange content as tiles or full-width bands. Keep corners square, or round controls by 4 px or less.
  • Keep contrast at 4.5:1 for body text. Put dark text on light hues such as turquoise and white text on dark hues.

Keep the function

  • Do not use gradients, gloss, bevels, inner shadows, or textures.
  • Do not add drop shadows to cards or buttons. Shadows turn the page into Material Design.
  • Do not outline cards and tiles. Outlines turn the page into a wireframe or neo-brutalism.
  • Do not remove every signifier from links and buttons. NN/g found that flat elements without cues cause click uncertainty.
  • Do not put white text on light hues such as turquoise or yellow.

Useful directions: mobile apps, dashboards, product and marketing sites, operating-system shells, infographics.
